An argument that leads to an overly general conclusion. A common test (this catalog's wording, not the cited source's): the same reasoning would also establish things the arguer would reject.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** We shouldn't fund the new library because some people never read (the same reasoning would rule out funding anything some people don't use).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An argument for a conclusion is given.
2. The same reasoning applies to cases where it yields a conclusion the arguer would reject (give one).
3. No relevant difference blocks that application.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A relevant difference between the cases is stated. *(catalog wording)*

**Related:** [False analogy](#false-analogy)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Proving too much". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies> Note: Wikipedia describes it only as an argument that results in an overly generalized conclusion; the 'would also prove things the arguer rejects' test is catalog wording.

`id: proving-too-much`

<a id="psychologists-fallacy"></a>
### Psychologist's fallacy

An observer assumes their own perspective is objective and reads it into the behaviour or experience they are studying.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** I would have felt humiliated in that situation, so the subject must have felt humiliated.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An observer describes someone else's experience or reasoning.
2. The observer's own perspective is attributed to the person observed. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. A conclusion depends on the attribution.

Condition 2 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Related, use only one per step** (projection): [Anthropomorphism](#anthropomorphism), [Pathetic fallacy](#pathetic-fallacy), [Reification](#reification), [Mind projection fallacy](#mind-projection), [Referential fallacy](#referential-fallacy), [Homunculus fallacy](#homunculus-fallacy)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Psychologist's fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: psychologists-fallacy`

<a id="question-begging-analogy"></a>
### Question-begging analogy

An argument by analogy whose force depends on the very point in dispute.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Eating meat is like eating people, so it's wrong.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An analogy is offered.
2. Whether the two cases are alike in the relevant respect is the very point in dispute.
3. The analogy is used to settle that point.

**Related, use only one per step** (circularity, comparison): [Begging the question](#begging-the-question), [Loaded label](#loaded-label), [Complex question](#complex-question), [Ideology-driven argumentation](#ideology-driven-argumentation), [False analogy](#false-analogy), [False equivalence](#false-equivalence), [False balance](#false-balance), [Dangling comparative](#dangling-comparative), [Package deal](#package-deal)

**Sources:**

- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Question-Begging Analogy". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/qbanalog.html>

`id: question-begging-analogy`

<a id="rationalization"></a>
### Rationalization

Offering reasons that are not the real reasons for a belief or action, chosen to make it look more acceptable.

Status: contested · Detectable from text: no

**Example:** I bought the sports car for its safety rating.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A reason is given for an action or belief.
2. The stated reason is not the actual reason. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. The real reason is hidden. *(may need facts outside the text)*

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A reason that may have come after the fact but is still sound; judge the reason on its merits. *(catalog wording)*
- Do not flag from the text alone; it needs independent evidence that the stated reason was not the real one. *(catalog wording)*

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Rationalization". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: rationalization`

<a id="secundum-quid"></a>
### Secundum quid

*Also called:* a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, ignoring qualifications

Aristotle's fallacy of treating something true only in a certain respect, or with a qualification, as if it were true without qualification.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** He's a good thief, and someone who is good is a good person, so he is a good person.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A claim is true only in some respect, at some time or with some qualification.
2. It is used as if it were true without qualification.
3. The conclusion relies on dropping the qualification.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The qualification does not affect the conclusion. *(catalog wording)*
- A rule applied to a genuine exception is accident; too few cases is hasty generalization. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive), chapter 5. <https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/sophist_refut.mb.txt>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "2.1.4 List and classification". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: secundum-quid`

<a id="self-fulfilling-prophecy"></a>
### Self-fulfilling prophecy

Treating the fulfilment of a prediction as confirming it, when the act of predicting helped bring the outcome about.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** I told everyone the bank would fail; the run on the bank proved me right.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A prediction is made.
2. Making or acting on it helped bring it about. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. Its coming true is cited as proof that it was right independently.

Condition 2 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: self-fulfilling-prophecy`

<a id="slippery-slope"></a>
### Slippery slope

*Also called:* domino fallacy, thin end of the wedge, camel's nose

Claiming that a first step will lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without good reason to think each step will actually follow.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** If we let students redo one test, soon they'll expect to redo every test, and degrees will be worthless.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A first step is opposed.
2. It is claimed to lead through a chain of steps to an undesirable result.
3. At least one step in the chain is given no adequate reason to think it likely. Evidence for the first link does not support later links, and a hedge ('probably') lowers the claimed probability but does not supply a missing link. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Condition 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Whether this is fallacious depends on how likely each step is; well-supported chains are reasonable. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Slippery Slope")*
- A chain of tiny vague steps with no practical prediction is line-drawing, not this. *(catalog wording)*
- When each later step needs a new decision by the same body, that step is not likely unless a binding mechanism (a precedent rule, a legal duty, bylaws) is shown. If one is shown, the step is supported. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (options and limits): [False dilemma](#false-dilemma), [Middle ground](#middle-ground), [Nirvana fallacy](#nirvana-fallacy), [Line-drawing fallacy](#line-drawing), [Vagueness (exploiting)](#vagueness)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Slippery Slope". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Domino". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Domino' as another name and points to the main entry.
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Slippery slope". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Slippery Slope". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/slipslop.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "1. The core fallacies". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: slippery-slope`

<a id="special-pleading"></a>
### Special pleading

*Also called:* double standard (one form)

Applying a rule or standard to others while exempting yourself or a favoured case without justifying the exception.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Everyone should obey the speed limit, but I'm a good driver, so I can go faster.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A general rule or standard is accepted.
2. An exception is claimed for one case.
3. No reason relevant to the rule's purpose is given for the exception; rank, convenience or 'I'm busy' do not count, and neither does a bare self-assessment that one meets the purpose the rule exists to verify ('I know I can be impartial').

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A relevant difference is stated and supported. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (consistency): [Inconsistency](#inconsistency), [Kettle logic](#kettle-logic), [Double standard](#double-standard)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Special Pleading". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Special pleading". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Special Pleading". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/specplea.html>

`id: special-pleading`

<a id="sunk-cost"></a>
### Sunk cost fallacy

*Also called:* sunk costs, Concorde fallacy

Continuing with something because of what has already been spent on it, rather than judging it on its future costs and benefits.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** We've already spent two years on this failing project, so we have to keep going.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A choice about what to do next is being made.
2. Past costs that cannot be recovered are cited.
3. They are treated as a reason to continue, independent of future costs and benefits.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Past investment as evidence about future prospects (for example, the project is nearly done). *(catalog wording)*
- Keeping a commitment for reasons of trust or reputation. *(catalog wording)*
- A real remaining benefit, or a real cost of switching, can be a reason to continue. *(catalog wording)*

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Sunk costs fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: sunk-cost`

<a id="superstitious-thinking"></a>
### Superstitious thinking

Treating omens, charms, rituals or similar grounds that are well known to be unreliable as reasons for a belief or as causes of events.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** A black cat crossed my path, so I'll cancel the interview.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A belief or prediction rests on omens, charms or similar grounds.
2. Those grounds are well known to be unreliable.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- If the reasoning is 'it followed, so it caused', use post hoc; if it claims thoughts or rituals act on the world, use magical thinking. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Superstitious Thinking". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: superstitious-thinking`

<a id="tokenism"></a>
### Tokenism

Accepting a token gesture as if it were an adequate substitute for real action.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The company planted ten trees, so it clearly cares about the environment.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A gesture or small step is offered.
2. It is presented as an adequate response to a problem.
3. It is clearly inadequate to the problem.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A small step openly offered as a first step. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (proportion): [Lack of proportion](#lack-of-proportion), [Exaggeration](#exaggeration), [Oversimplification](#oversimplification), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Quibbling](#quibbling)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Tokenism". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: tokenism`

<a id="unfalsifiability"></a>
### Unfalsifiability

*Also called:* untestability, self-sealing argument

Offering an explanation of events that no possible observation could count against, and treating that as a strength of the explanation.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The cure works for those with enough faith; if it didn't work for you, your faith was too weak.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A claim is offered as an empirical claim about the world.
2. It is framed so that no possible observation could count against it.
3. It is still presented as established or explanatory, although its framing, not evidence, is what protects it from refutation.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Definitions, mathematics, logical truths and value claims, which are not offered as explanations of events. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (rescuing a claim): [Ad hoc rescue](#ad-hoc-rescue), [No true Scotsman](#no-true-scotsman), [Hedging](#hedging), [Moving the goalposts](#moving-the-goalposts), [Definitional retreat](#definitional-retreat), [Motte-and-bailey](#motte-and-bailey), [Far-fetched hypothesis](#far-fetched-hypothesis)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Unfalsifiability". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Untestability". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Untestability' as another name and points to the main entry.

`id: unfalsifiability`

<a id="vacuous-truth"></a>
### Vacuous truth (misuse)

Offering a claim that is technically true only because there is nothing for it to be about, as if it were informative.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** None of our cars have ever failed a safety test (we've never had one tested).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A universal claim is offered as informative.
2. It is true only because the class it is about is empty.

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Vacuous truth". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: vacuous-truth`

<a id="willed-ignorance"></a>
### Willed ignorance

*Also called:* invincible ignorance, argument by pigheadedness

Openly refusing to look at, or respond to, evidence or arguments against a view one has already decided to hold.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** I've decided the treatment works, and I'm not reading any more studies about it.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A view is held.
2. Counterevidence or arguments are pointed out.
3. The speaker openly refuses to look at or respond to them.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Declining to revisit something already thoroughly considered, with a reason. *(catalog wording)*
- Remaining unconvinced after looking at the evidence. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (bare assertion): [Ipse dixit](#ipse-dixit), [Proof by assertion](#proof-by-assertion), [Argument from repetition](#argument-from-repetition), [Thought-terminating cliché](#thought-terminating-cliche), [Appeal to the stone](#appeal-to-the-stone), [I'm entitled to my opinion](#entitled-to-my-opinion), [Proof surrogate](#proof-surrogate), [Appeal to ridicule](#appeal-to-ridicule), [Subjectivist fallacy](#subjectivist-fallacy)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Willed ignorance". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies", item "Invincible ignorance". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: willed-ignorance`

## Informal: weak induction

<a id="anecdotal-evidence"></a>
### Anecdotal evidence

*Also called:* anecdotal fallacy, argument from anecdote, volvo fallacy

Relying on a personal story or a few vivid cases instead of more representative evidence.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that harmful.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A conclusion about a general pattern is drawn.
2. The evidence offered is one or a few personal stories, or unsystematic personal impressions.
3. Better systematic evidence exists or would be needed for the conclusion. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Condition 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- An anecdote used to illustrate a pattern established on other grounds, or to show that something is possible. *(catalog wording)*
- Long, systematically recorded professional observation (for example, a clinic's own logged case series) is not mere anecdote. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Anecdotal Evidence". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Argument from anecdote". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "The Anecdotal Fallacy". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/volvofal.html>

`id: anecdotal-evidence`

<a id="argument-from-ignorance"></a>
### Argument from ignorance

*Also called:* appeal to ignorance, argumentum ad ignorantiam

Treating a lack of disproof as proof, or a lack of proof as disproof.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** No one has proved that ghosts don't exist, so they do.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A claim has not been proven false (or true).
2. It is concluded to be true (or false) on that basis.
3. Nothing in the context shows a thorough search was made where evidence would be expected if the claim were true.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A thorough search was done and a proof would have been found if it existed. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Appeal to Ignorance")*
- A procedural default or burden rule established independently of this argument (a law, regulation, a null hypothesis or a house rule set beforehand), with the conclusion kept to a decision about what to do rather than asserting that the claim is false. It does not apply if an established standard exists and points the other way. *(catalog wording)*
- A precautionary decision under uncertainty, stated as a decision, with the costs of being wrong either way weighed. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (ignorance and burden): [Misplaced burden of proof](#misplaced-burden-of-proof), [Argument from silence](#argument-from-silence), [Argument from incredulity](#argument-from-incredulity)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Appeal to Ignorance". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Argument from Ignorance". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Argument from Ignorance' as another name and points to the main entry.
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies", item "Argument from ignorance". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Appeal to Ignorance". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "2.4 Locke". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: argument-from-ignorance`

<a id="argument-from-incredulity"></a>
### Argument from incredulity

*Also called:* argument from personal incredulity, divine fallacy

Concluding that something is false (or must have an extraordinary cause) because you find it hard to believe or imagine.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** I can't imagine how an eye could evolve, so it couldn't have.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. The speaker says they cannot imagine or believe how something could be so.
2. It is concluded that it is false.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Disbelief backed by a specific reason why the claim is implausible. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (ignorance and burden): [Argument from ignorance](#argument-from-ignorance), [Misplaced burden of proof](#misplaced-burden-of-proof), [Argument from silence](#argument-from-silence)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Argument from incredulity". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Divine fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: argument-from-incredulity`

<a id="argument-from-silence"></a>
### Argument from silence

*Also called:* argumentum ex silentio

Drawing a conclusion from the absence of a statement or record, when that absence has other likely explanations.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** His diary never mentions his brother, so he didn't have one.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A source does not mention something.
2. It is concluded that the thing did not happen or the author did not know of it.
3. There is no strong reason to expect the source would have mentioned it. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Condition 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The source would very likely have mentioned it if it were so. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (ignorance and burden): [Argument from ignorance](#argument-from-ignorance), [Misplaced burden of proof](#misplaced-burden-of-proof), [Argument from incredulity](#argument-from-incredulity)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies", item "Argument from silence". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: argument-from-silence`

<a id="cherry-picking"></a>
### Cherry-picking

*Also called:* cherry picking, selective use of evidence, fallacy of exclusion

Drawing a conclusion from a selected part of the evidence while the rest of it, which is stated or plainly known, points the other way or weakens it and goes unanswered. Unlike suppressed evidence, the contrary evidence is in plain view.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The report shows test scores rose at three of the ten pilot schools and fell at the other seven. The programme clearly works: look at those three schools.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. The arguer selects a subset of the available or stated data. This includes choosing a measurement period while the arguer's own stated record extends beyond it.
2. The rest of the data, stated or plainly known, points the other way or dilutes the subset; or a comparative claim is made with no comparison figure while the chosen window excludes stated history.
3. The conclusion rests on the subset, and the rest gets no answer.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The subset is singled out for a stated, independent reason (for example, a subgroup named before the data came in). *(catalog wording)*
- Highlighting the strongest examples while acknowledging and answering the rest. *(catalog wording)*
- If the contrary evidence is absent from the text, use suppressed evidence instead. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (omitted evidence, selective evidence): [Suppressed evidence](#suppressed-evidence), [Nut-picking](#nut-picking), [Selective attention](#selective-attention), [Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)](#confirmation-bias), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science), [Survivorship bias](#survivorship-bias), [Quoting out of context](#quoting-out-of-context), [Overwhelming exception](#overwhelming-exception), [Texas sharpshooter fallacy](#texas-sharpshooter), [Lottery fallacy](#lottery-fallacy)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Cherry picking". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Cherry-Picking". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP treats cherry-picking as another name for suppressed evidence; this catalog keeps a separate entry for the case where the contrary evidence is in plain view.

`id: cherry-picking`

<a id="converse-accident"></a>
### Converse accident

*Also called:* reverse accident, generalizing from the exception

Generalizing from exceptional cases to a rule meant for ordinary cases.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Patients in pain are allowed morphine, so everyone should be allowed morphine.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Atypical or exceptional cases are cited.
2. A general rule or claim for ordinary cases is drawn from them.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Deliberately setting a rule that covers the exceptions as a separate category. *(catalog wording)*
- Do not also tag hasty generalization for the same step. *(catalog wording)*
- If one ordinary case is carried over to another comparable case (no exception involved), use false analogy. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion), [False analogy](#false-analogy)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Converse Accident". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Hasty Generalization". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/hastygen.html> Note: The Fallacy Files lists converse accident as another name for hasty generalization.

`id: converse-accident`

<a id="false-analogy"></a>
### False analogy

*Also called:* weak analogy, faulty analogy, questionable analogy, improper analogy, faulty comparison, apples and oranges

Arguing that because two things are alike in some ways they are alike in another way, when the similarities are not relevant to that point or the differences matter more.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Employees are like nails: they work best when you hit them on the head.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Two things are compared.
2. A conclusion about one is drawn from the other.
3. They differ in a respect relevant to the conclusion (state it).

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- An analogy where the shared features are the ones that matter to the conclusion. *(catalog wording)*
- An analogy used to illustrate, not to argue. *(catalog wording)*
- If the source case is an exception (a special population or special circumstances) and the conclusion is a rule for ordinary cases or for everyone, use converse accident. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (comparison): [False equivalence](#false-equivalence), [False balance](#false-balance), [Question-begging analogy](#question-begging-analogy), [Dangling comparative](#dangling-comparative), [Package deal](#package-deal), [Proving too much](#proving-too-much), [Converse accident](#converse-accident)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Analogy". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Weak Analogy". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Weak Analogy' as another name and points to the main entry.
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "False analogy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Weak Analogy". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/wanalogy.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "1. The core fallacies". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Faulty Comparison". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: lists this under the name 'Faulty comparison'.

`id: false-analogy`

<a id="feedback-fallacy"></a>
### Feedback fallacy

Trusting an evaluation as objective, and acting on it, without checking whether its source is disinterested.

Status: contested · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** My manager says I'm the problem, so I must be (the manager is defending his own decisions).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An evaluation (feedback, a review) is relied on.
2. Its source has an interest or bias that is not checked. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. It is treated as objective.

Condition 2 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A reviewer's stake is a reason to check the evaluation, not proof that it is wrong. *(catalog wording)*

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Feedback fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: feedback-fallacy`

<a id="hasty-generalization"></a>
### Hasty generalization

*Also called:* small sample, insufficient statistics, fallacy of insufficient sample, hasty induction, lonely fact

Drawing a general conclusion from too few cases to support it.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** My two neighbours from that city were rude, so people from that city are rude.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A general conclusion about a group is drawn.
2. The evidence is a sample of the group.
3. The sample is too small, or the conclusion is too sweeping, for the evidence.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A small sample can suffice when the population is known to be uniform in the relevant respect. *(catalog wording)*
- A tentative conclusion stated with appropriate caution. *(catalog wording)*
- Do not also tag converse accident or secundum quid for the same step. *(catalog wording)*
- A small sample with a large, consistent effect, used for a reversible or low-stakes decision. *(catalog wording)*
- If the doubt is about how the sample was chosen rather than its size, use unrepresentative sample. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hasty Generalization". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Small Sample". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Insufficient Statistics". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Hasty generalization". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Hasty Generalization". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/hastygen.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "2.3 Arnauld and Nicole". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: hasty-generalization`

<a id="inductive-conversion"></a>
### Inductive conversion

Reasoning from 'all (or most) A are B' to 'all (or most) B are A'.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Most jockeys are short, so most short people are jockeys.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. It is accepted that all or most A are B.
2. It is concluded that all or most B are A.

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Inductive Conversion". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: inductive-conversion`

<a id="inflation-of-conflict"></a>
### Inflation of conflict

Arguing that because experts disagree on some point, nothing can be known in that field or the field as a whole is unreliable.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Economists argue about interest rates, so economics is just guesswork.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Experts are shown to disagree on some point.
2. It is concluded that nothing can be known in the field, or that the field is unreliable as a whole.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Concluding that the specific point in dispute is unsettled. *(catalog wording)*
- If the claim simply conflicts with well-established findings and the conflict is not addressed, use disregarding known science. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (authority and popularity): [Appeal to authority (illegitimate)](#appeal-to-authority), [Appeal to celebrity](#appeal-to-celebrity), [Appeal to accomplishment](#appeal-to-accomplishment), [Appeal to the people](#appeal-to-the-people), [Bandwagon](#bandwagon), [Appeal to tradition](#appeal-to-tradition), [Appeal to novelty](#appeal-to-novelty), [Group think](#group-think), [Chronological snobbery](#chronological-snobbery), [Appeal to wealth](#appeal-to-wealth), [Appeal to poverty](#appeal-to-poverty), [Appeal to sincerity](#appeal-to-sincerity), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Inflation of conflict". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: inflation-of-conflict`

<a id="jumping-to-conclusions"></a>
### Jumping to conclusions

*Also called:* hasty conclusion

Reaching a conclusion without relevant evidence that was readily available, when there was time and it was practical to get it.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly · Fallback: use only if nothing more specific fits

**Example:** The lights are off at her house, so she must have moved away.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A conclusion is drawn.
2. Relevant evidence was not gathered or considered. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. There was time and opportunity to do so. *(may need facts outside the text)*
4. No more specific entry fits.

Conditions 2, 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Quick decisions are not always wrong; it is the fallacy only when there was time and the effort was not prohibitive. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Jumping to Conclusions")*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Jumping to Conclusions". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hasty Conclusion". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Hasty Conclusion' as another name and points to the main entry.

`id: jumping-to-conclusions`

<a id="misleading-vividness"></a>
### Misleading vividness

Letting a few dramatic, memorable cases outweigh a larger body of statistical evidence.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** I saw a terrible shark attack on the news, so swimming at the beach is too dangerous, whatever the statistics say.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A vivid, memorable case is described.
2. It is used to support a claim about how common or likely something is.
3. Statistical evidence pointing the other way exists (stated, or well known) and is outweighed or ignored. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Condition 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A vivid case used as an illustration of a pattern shown by the statistics. *(catalog wording)*
- Pick one of misleading vividness or anecdotal evidence for a given step. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misleading Vividness". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: misleading-vividness`

<a id="nut-picking"></a>
### Nut-picking

*Also called:* nutpicking

Finding the most extreme or fringe members of an opposing group and presenting them as typical of the whole group.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Look at this one ranting post; that's what all supporters of that policy are like.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Statements by a group's most extreme members are cited.
2. They are presented as representing the whole group.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Examples that are shown to be typical. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (omitted evidence): [Suppressed evidence](#suppressed-evidence), [Selective attention](#selective-attention), [Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)](#confirmation-bias), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science), [Survivorship bias](#survivorship-bias), [Quoting out of context](#quoting-out-of-context), [Overwhelming exception](#overwhelming-exception), [Cherry-picking](#cherry-picking)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Nut-picking". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: nut-picking`

<a id="overwhelming-exception"></a>
### Overwhelming exception

A generalization stated with so many qualifications that what is left is much weaker than the headline claim suggests.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** All our customers are satisfied, apart from those who complained, returned the product, or didn't respond.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A general claim is made.
2. It is qualified with so many exceptions that little is left.
3. It is still presented as the strong headline claim.

**Related, use only one per step** (omitted evidence): [Suppressed evidence](#suppressed-evidence), [Nut-picking](#nut-picking), [Selective attention](#selective-attention), [Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)](#confirmation-bias), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science), [Survivorship bias](#survivorship-bias), [Quoting out of context](#quoting-out-of-context), [Cherry-picking](#cherry-picking)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Overwhelming exception". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: overwhelming-exception`

<a id="proof-surrogate"></a>
### Proof surrogate

Substituting a phrase that suggests proof, such as 'everyone knows' or 'studies show', for actual evidence.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Any reasonable person can see the plan is sound, and experts agree.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A claim is made.
2. A phrase suggesting proof ('studies show', 'everyone knows') is used.
3. No actual evidence is given or identified.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The phrase is accompanied by a checkable citation. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (bare assertion): [Ipse dixit](#ipse-dixit), [Proof by assertion](#proof-by-assertion), [Argument from repetition](#argument-from-repetition), [Thought-terminating cliché](#thought-terminating-cliche), [Appeal to the stone](#appeal-to-the-stone), [I'm entitled to my opinion](#entitled-to-my-opinion), [Appeal to ridicule](#appeal-to-ridicule), [Subjectivist fallacy](#subjectivist-fallacy), [Willed ignorance](#willed-ignorance)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Proof Surrogate". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: proof-surrogate`

<a id="selective-attention"></a>
### Selective attention

Focusing on some aspects of a situation while ignoring others that are relevant.

Status: contested · Detectable from text: no

**Example:** 'How was school?' 'I got an A in art!' (the four failed tests go unmentioned).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A conclusion is drawn from observations.
2. Only observations fitting an expectation were noticed. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. Contrary observations were available. *(may need facts outside the text)*

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- If the text omits known contrary evidence, consider suppressed evidence. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (omitted evidence): [Suppressed evidence](#suppressed-evidence), [Nut-picking](#nut-picking), [Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)](#confirmation-bias), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science), [Survivorship bias](#survivorship-bias), [Quoting out of context](#quoting-out-of-context), [Overwhelming exception](#overwhelming-exception), [Cherry-picking](#cherry-picking)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Selective Attention". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: selective-attention`

<a id="specificity"></a>
### Specificity

Drawing a more specific conclusion than the evidence supports.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The trails were dug by an animal, so a badger dug them last Tuesday night.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A conclusion is drawn.
2. It is more specific than the evidence supports (for example, naming one cause when evidence only shows some cause).

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Do not also tag jumping to conclusions. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Specificity". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: specificity`

<a id="stereotyping"></a>
### Stereotyping

Applying a group image to an individual member, or to every member, as if it were a reliable rule, without evidence about that individual.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** She's an accountant, so she must be boring.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A trait is attributed to a group.
2. It is applied to an individual member.
3. The individual's own characteristics are not considered, or the group claim lacks adequate evidence.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Reasoning from well-supported group rates to a probability, when no individual information is available, and stating it as a probability. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)](#availability-heuristic), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Stereotyping". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: stereotyping`

<a id="suppressed-evidence"></a>
### Suppressed evidence

*Also called:* card stacking, stacking the deck, one-sidedness, ignoring the counterevidence, ignoring inconvenient data, incomplete evidence, cover-up, argument by half-truth, slanting

Leaving out evidence that is significant and would weaken the conclusion, when the arguer had it or should have had it, and presenting the case as if it were complete.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** Our drug helped 30 patients (we won't mention the 70 it didn't).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An argument presents evidence for a conclusion.
2. Relevant, significant evidence against it is omitted (identify it). *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. The arguer knew or should have known of it. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Conditions 2, 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The omitted evidence is not significant, or the arguer could not have known it. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Suppressed Evidence")*
- An openly one-sided brief in an adversarial setting where the other side presents its case. *(catalog wording)*
- A short case that does not claim to be complete. *(catalog wording)*
- If the contrary evidence is stated in the passage (or plainly known) and simply ignored, use cherry-picking. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (omitted evidence, selective evidence): [Nut-picking](#nut-picking), [Selective attention](#selective-attention), [Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)](#confirmation-bias), [Disregarding known science](#disregarding-known-science), [Survivorship bias](#survivorship-bias), [Quoting out of context](#quoting-out-of-context), [Overwhelming exception](#overwhelming-exception), [Cherry-picking](#cherry-picking), [Texas sharpshooter fallacy](#texas-sharpshooter), [Lottery fallacy](#lottery-fallacy)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Suppressed Evidence". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Cherry picking". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies> Note: Wikipedia lists suppressed evidence as another name for cherry picking.
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "One-Sidedness". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/onesided.html>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Slanting". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: lists this under the name 'Slanting'.

`id: suppressed-evidence`

## Informal: causal

<a id="cum-hoc"></a>
### Cum hoc ergo propter hoc

*Also called:* correlation implies causation, with this, therefore because of this

Concluding that because two things occur together, one causes the other.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, so ice cream causes drowning.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Two things are shown to occur together (a correlation).
2. One is concluded to cause the other.
3. At least one plausible alternative (chance, a third factor, the reverse direction) is left open, and the causal claim is stated as established rather than as a hypothesis to test.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Correlations are often good evidence of causation when alternatives are addressed. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Post Hoc")*
- A correlation can support a causal conclusion once coincidence, a confounding cause and the reverse direction have been ruled out. *(source: Fallacy Files, entry "Cum Hoc, Ergo Propter Hoc")*
- A correlation plus a comparison group or a known mechanism, offered as grounds to investigate. *(catalog wording)*
- If the argument does address causes but misses an obvious third factor, use ignoring a common cause. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Cum Hoc, Ergo Propter Hoc". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Cum hoc ergo propter hoc". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Cum Hoc, Ergo Propter Hoc". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/cumhocfa.html>

`id: cum-hoc`

<a id="single-cause"></a>
### Fallacy of the single cause

*Also called:* causal oversimplification, complex cause

Assuming an outcome has one simple cause when it actually arose from several causes acting together.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The war started because an archduke was shot.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An outcome is attributed to one cause.
2. Other contributing causes are known or evident (name one).
3. The conclusion relies on the single cause being the whole story.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Picking out the most important or most controllable cause while acknowledging others. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation, proportion): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox), [Lack of proportion](#lack-of-proportion), [Exaggeration](#exaggeration), [Oversimplification](#oversimplification), [Tokenism](#tokenism), [Quibbling](#quibbling)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Fallacy of the single cause". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: single-cause`

<a id="false-cause"></a>
### False cause

*Also called:* non causa pro causa, questionable cause

Concluding that one thing causes another when the only support is that they occur together or in sequence, or when an obvious alternative explanation (a common cause, reversed direction, or chance) has not been ruled out.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes · Fallback: use only if nothing more specific fits

**Example:** Countries with more Nobel laureates eat more chocolate, so chocolate makes people smarter.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A causal conclusion is drawn.
2. The only support is that the two occur together or in sequence, or an obvious alternative (a common cause, the reverse direction, chance) is left open.
3. No more specific causal entry (post hoc, correlation, common cause, reverse causation, single cause, regression) fits.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A tentative causal hypothesis offered for testing. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation, non-cause: ancient and modern): [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox), [Non-cause (Aristotle's sense)](#non-cause-aristotle), [Inconsistency](#inconsistency)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "False Cause". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Non Causa Pro Causa". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Non Causa Pro Causa". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/noncause.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "2.3 Arnauld and Nicole". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: false-cause`

<a id="furtive-fallacy"></a>
### Furtive fallacy

Assuming that outcomes must have been caused by the hidden wrongdoing of people in charge.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** The project failed, so someone must have sabotaged it.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. An outcome is explained by hidden wrongdoing by people in charge.
2. No evidence of the wrongdoing is given.
3. Ordinary explanations are not considered. *(may need facts outside the text)*

Condition 3 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Wrongdoing alleged with evidence. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Furtive fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: furtive-fallacy`

<a id="common-cause"></a>
### Ignoring a common cause

*Also called:* neglecting a common cause, third-cause fallacy, common cause

Concluding that A causes B when both are actually caused by some third factor.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** Children with bigger feet read better, so big feet improve reading (both come with age).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. One thing is said to cause another.
2. A third factor plausibly causes both (name it). *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. The argument does not address it.

Condition 2 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Raise as an issue only when there is some evidence of a common cause, not merely possibility. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Common Cause")*
- An obvious common-knowledge third factor (rain causing both wiper use and accidents) counts as 'some evidence' of a common cause. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Common Cause". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Neglecting a Common Cause". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/> Note: IEP lists 'Neglecting a Common Cause' as another name and points to the main entry.
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Ignoring a common cause". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: common-cause`

<a id="magical-thinking"></a>
### Magical thinking

Assuming a causal link between events that have no plausible connection, such as between thoughts, rituals or symbols and outside events.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** If I think about the accident, it might happen.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A causal link is claimed between thoughts, words, rituals or symbols and outside events.
2. There is no plausible mechanism, and the conclusion relies on the link.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Rituals valued for their psychological effect on the person doing them. *(catalog wording)*
- If the reasoning is only 'it followed, so it caused', use post hoc. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Magical thinking". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: magical-thinking`

<a id="post-hoc"></a>
### Post hoc ergo propter hoc

*Also called:* post hoc, after this, therefore because of this

Concluding that because B happened after A, A caused B.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks helped us win.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. One event followed another.
2. The first is concluded to have caused the second.
3. The order in time is the main or only evidence offered.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Sequence is some evidence of cause; the fallacy is the hasty leap, not considering timing. *(source: IEP, section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Post Hoc")*
- Timing plus a known mechanism or controlled comparison. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Post Hoc". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Post hoc ergo propter hoc". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "Post Hoc". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/posthocf.html>
- Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Hans Hansen), section "1. The core fallacies". <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/>

`id: post-hoc`

<a id="retrospective-determinism"></a>
### Retrospective determinism

Assuming that because something happened under certain circumstances, those circumstances made it inevitable.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The company collapsed, so its collapse was bound to happen from the day it was founded.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Something happened under certain circumstances.
2. It is concluded that those circumstances made it inevitable.
3. No reason is given why it could not have turned out otherwise.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- A demonstrated mechanism that left no alternative. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation, history): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Reversing causation](#reverse-causation), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox), [Historian's fallacy](#historians-fallacy), [Historical fallacy](#historical-fallacy), [Baconian fallacy](#baconian-fallacy)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies", item "Retrospective determinism". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: retrospective-determinism`

<a id="reverse-causation"></a>
### Reversing causation

*Also called:* wrong direction, reverse causation

Getting cause and effect the wrong way round.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Hospitals are full of sick people, so hospitals make people sick.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A link between A and B is observed.
2. A is concluded to cause B.
3. B plausibly causes A instead, and this is not addressed.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Two-way causation, or a reverse direction ruled out by timing or design. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (causation): [False cause](#false-cause), [Post hoc ergo propter hoc](#post-hoc), [Cum hoc ergo propter hoc](#cum-hoc), [Ignoring a common cause](#common-cause), [Fallacy of the single cause](#single-cause), [Regression fallacy](#regression-fallacy), [Observational interpretation fallacy](#observational-interpretation), [Superstitious thinking](#superstitious-thinking), [Magical thinking](#magical-thinking), [Furtive fallacy](#furtive-fallacy), [Retrospective determinism](#retrospective-determinism), [Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal)](#simpsons-paradox)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Reversing Causation". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>
- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause", item "Wrong direction". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: reverse-causation`

## Informal: statistical and probabilistic

<a id="appeal-to-probability"></a>
### Appeal to probability

*Also called:* appeal to possibility

Treating something that merely could happen as if it will happen, or something that is likely as if it were certain.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Someone could hack this account, so someone will.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. Something is said to be possible, or likely.
2. It is then treated as certain or as sure to happen.
3. The conclusion depends on that upgrade.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Acting with caution on a well-founded probability ('it could happen, so let's insure'). *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (probability): [Base-rate fallacy](#base-rate-fallacy), [Prosecutor's fallacy](#prosecutors-fallacy), [Conjunction fallacy](#conjunction-fallacy), [Independence fallacy](#independence-fallacy), [Double counting](#double-counting), [Confusion of the inverse](#confusion-of-the-inverse)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Formal fallacies", item "Appeal to probability". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>

`id: appeal-to-probability`

<a id="availability-heuristic"></a>
### Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)

*Also called:* availability error

Judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, and deciding on that basis.

Status: contested · Detectable from text: no

**Example:** I'll drive instead of flying; you always hear about plane crashes.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A judgement about how common or likely something is is made.
2. The judgement rests on how easily memorable examples come to mind. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. Actual frequency data are available and point the other way. *(may need facts outside the text)*

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- Recall of cases that really are typical. If the text cites a vivid case as its reason, use misleading vividness instead. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (generalization): [Accident](#accident), [Secundum quid](#secundum-quid), [Hasty generalization](#hasty-generalization), [Converse accident](#converse-accident), [Anecdotal evidence](#anecdotal-evidence), [Misleading vividness](#misleading-vividness), [Unrepresentative sample](#unrepresentative-sample), [Stereotyping](#stereotyping), [Jumping to conclusions](#jumping-to-conclusions), [Specificity](#specificity), [Overgenerality](#overgenerality), [Inductive conversion](#inductive-conversion)

**Sources:**

- Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden), section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Availability Heuristic". <https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/>

`id: availability-heuristic`

<a id="base-rate-fallacy"></a>
### Base-rate fallacy

*Also called:* base-rate neglect, neglecting base rates

Judging a probability from specific evidence (such as a test result) while ignoring how common the thing is to begin with.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: partly

**Example:** The test is 99% accurate and I tested positive, so I almost certainly have this disease that affects 1 in 100,000 people.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A probability about a specific case is estimated from specific evidence such as a test result or description.
2. The base rate (how common the thing is overall) is relevant and is known or knowable. *(may need facts outside the text)*
3. The estimate ignores or badly underweights that base rate.

Condition 2 may need facts outside the text. Each is met if the passage states the fact or it is common knowledge; otherwise record possible issue and name the fact that would settle it.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The base rate is unknown and the speaker says so. *(catalog wording)*
- The specific evidence is so strong that the base rate makes little difference, and this is shown. *(catalog wording)*
- If 'the chance of this evidence if innocent' is presented as the chance of innocence, use prosecutor's fallacy. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (probability): [Prosecutor's fallacy](#prosecutors-fallacy), [Conjunction fallacy](#conjunction-fallacy), [Independence fallacy](#independence-fallacy), [Appeal to probability](#appeal-to-probability), [Double counting](#double-counting), [Confusion of the inverse](#confusion-of-the-inverse)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "List of fallacies", section "Formal fallacies", item "Base rate fallacy". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fallacies>
- The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis), entry "The Base Rate Fallacy". <https://www.fallacyfiles.org/baserate.html>

`id: base-rate-fallacy`

<a id="statistical-vs-practical-significance"></a>
### Confusing statistical with practical significance

*Also called:* statistical significance taken as importance

Treating a statistically significant result as if it showed a large or important effect. Statistical significance says how unlikely the result would be by chance alone, not how big the effect is.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** The trial found the new diet led to statistically significant weight loss, so it is a major breakthrough for people trying to slim down (the average loss was 0.4 kg in a year).

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. A result is called statistically significant.
2. It is presented as large, important or worth acting on.
3. The stated effect size is too small to support that, or no effect size is given and the claim of importance rests on the word 'significant' alone.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- The effect size is reported and is large enough for the stated use. *(catalog wording)*
- Reporting that a result is statistically significant, without claiming that it is large or important. *(catalog wording)*

**Related, use only one per step** (reporting numbers): [Relative-risk framing (absolute risk left out)](#relative-risk-framing), [Fallacy of the sheep](#fallacy-of-the-sheep), [Fake precision](#fake-precision)

**Sources:**

- Wikipedia, "Misuse of statistics", article "Misuse of statistics", section "Confusing statistical significance with practical significance". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misuse_of_statistics>
- Wikipedia, "Clinical significance", article "Clinical significance", section "Types of significance > Practical significance". <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_significance>

`id: statistical-vs-practical-significance`

<a id="confusion-of-the-inverse"></a>
### Confusion of the inverse

*Also called:* inverse fallacy, conditional probability fallacy

Treating the chance of a feature given a hypothesis as if it were the chance of the hypothesis given the feature: from 'all or most H have E' and 'this case has E', concluding that it is (probably) H, without asking how common E is among cases that are not H.

Status: standard · Detectable from text: yes

**Example:** Nearly every fake charity we've exposed used urgent deadlines and pushy phone calls. This charity uses urgent deadlines and pushy calls, so it's probably fake.

**Required conditions** (all must be shown from the text):

1. The passage states or relies on: all or most H have feature E.
2. A case with E is concluded to be H, or probably H.
3. Nothing is given or used about how common E is among cases that are not H.

**Legitimate look-alikes** (not this fallacy):

- How common E is outside H is given or used, and E is shown to be rare outside H, so the inference is weighed properly. *(catalog wording)*
- If the error is ignoring how common H is overall when reading a test result, use base-rate fallacy; if 'the chance of this evidence if innocent' is presented as the chance of innocence, use prosecutor's fallacy. *(catalog wording)*
